Identity.History:
Liu Che, better known as Emperor Wu of Han, ruled from 141 to 87 BCE and transformed the Han state into a much more powerful and expansive empire. He strengthened the authority of the central government, reduced the independence of regional kings, and promoted a more ideologically unified imperial order. His reign also saw increased state sponsorship of Confucian learning, although Han government continued to incorporate ideas and administrative practices drawn from several intellectual traditions.
Emperor Wu pursued an aggressive foreign policy, especially against the Xiongnu. Under generals such as Wei Qing and Huo Qubing, Han armies launched major cavalry campaigns deep into the northern steppe. Han power also expanded into the Hexi Corridor, Central Asian regions, Korea, and parts of the south and southwest. Diplomatic missions associated with Zhang Qian opened stronger connections with Central Asia and contributed to the development of long-distance trade networks later grouped under the name Silk Road.
These ambitions placed enormous demands on the empire. To finance warfare and administration, Emperor Wu expanded taxation and introduced or strengthened state control over industries such as salt and iron. His later reign was troubled by court intrigue, heavy burdens on the population, and the disastrous witchcraft persecutions that culminated in the rebellion and death of Crown Prince Liu Ju. Even so, Emperor Wu left behind a greatly enlarged empire and a model of centralized imperial power that profoundly influenced later Chinese rulers.
